prompt.context: Robot & Company (Robot Co.) is a company headquartered in California, USA and Shenzhen, China — two important world capitals for hardware innovation. In early 2020 the catering industry has undergone significant change, especially with the outbreak of Covid-19. Robot Co. is catching up with the market trend by rolling out the Gundam-II, a robot specifically designed to deliver dishes and drinks from the kitchen to the dining area. The robot executes orders in the system instantly and disinfects itself at the end of each mission; the disinfection lasts 5 seconds each time. The CEO of Robot Co. has tasked us with figuring out whether to launch Gundam-II in Singapore, and how to price this new product.
prompt.question: Should Robot Co. launch Gundam-II in Singapore, and how should it price the product? The interviewer will walk you through four structured questions on this topic.

clarifying_info.q: Where are Robot Co.'s operations located?
clarifying_info.a: R&D is in California and Shenzhen; manufacturing plant is in Shenzhen; sales network covers North America, North Asia, and Southeast Asia.

clarifying_info.q: Does Robot Co. have competitors for Gundam-II?
clarifying_info.a: Gundam-II is patented and Robot Co. has strong technical leadership. No potential competitors are expected in the foreseeable 2-5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the business model — sell or lease?
clarifying_info.a: Robot Co. plans to lease Gundam-II to restaurants for a monthly rental payment rather than selling outright.

clarifying_info.q: Why would restaurants want this product?
clarifying_info.a: No-contact service has become fashionable in restaurants — it reduces the risk of virus transmission and helps management reduce labor costs.

exhibits.title: Dimension of Gundam-II at Full Capacity
exhibits.shows: A diagram showing the maximum loadable volume of Gundam-II at full capacity and the outer packaging dimensions of Super Drink.
exhibits.data: Gundam-II maximum loadable volume: 20 x 21 x 35 inches. Super Drink outer packaging: 5 x 7 x 4 inches.

exhibits.title: Efficiency of Gundam-II vs. Server
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the time (in minutes) Gundam-II and a human server each spend on three tasks to serve a standard meal of 4 customers.
exhibits.data: Pick up dishes & beverages: Gundam-II 1.5 min x 1 time = 1.5 min; Server 2 min x 4 times = 8 min. Deliver dishes & beverages: Gundam-II 2.5 min x 1 time = 2.5 min; Server 1.5 min x 4 times = 6 min. Place dishes & beverages: Gundam-II 1 min x 4 times = 4 min; Server 1 min x 4 times = 4 min. Total: Gundam-II 8 min; Server 16 min.

framework: This is an interviewer-led case with four discrete questions — no single overarching framework is required
Q1: Spatial/volume math puzzle (packing Gundam-II cargo hold with Super Drink boxes)
Q2: Pricing strategy — anchor on cost-based floor, then derive value-based ceiling from labor savings; recommend value-based given competitive moat
Q3: Market sizing — estimate Singapore full-service restaurant universe, servers per restaurant, conversion rate, and monthly rental to reach annual market size
Q4: Risk identification and mitigation — regulation, operational, and public perception risks

questions.prompt: Q1 — The Gundam-II's loading capacity is adjustable and its maximum loadable volume is 20 x 21 x 35 inches. Super Drink has an outer packaging size of 5 x 7 x 4 inches. With the Gundam-II at full capacity (and able to adjust the orientation of packages), what is the maximum number of Super Drink units that can be transported at one time?
questions.guidance: The trick is to try multiple packing orientations and pick the best. Candidates who blindly divide volumes (20x21x35 / 5x7x4 = 14700/140 = 105) may accidentally get the right answer, but the correct reasoning is to test orientations dimension-by-dimension. The answer is 105, not 102 (a common wrong answer). A strong candidate systematically tries orientations and correctly identifies 105.

math.setup: Gundam-II hold: 20 x 21 x 35 inches. Super Drink box: 5 x 7 x 4 inches. Find the orientation that maximises integer packing along each axis.
steps: Orientation A (5 along 20, 7 along 21, 4 along 35): floor(20/5)=4, floor(21/7)=3, floor(35/4)=8 -> 4x3x8=96
Orientation B (5 along 20, 4 along 21, 7 along 35): floor(20/5)=4, floor(21/4)=5, floor(35/7)=5 -> 4x5x5=100
Orientation C (7 along 20, 5 along 21, 4 along 35): floor(20/7)=2, floor(21/5)=4, floor(35/4)=8 -> 2x4x8=64
Orientation D (7 along 20, 4 along 21, 5 along 35): floor(20/7)=2, floor(21/4)=5, floor(35/5)=7 -> 2x5x7=70
Orientation E (4 along 20, 5 along 21, 7 along 35): floor(20/4)=5, floor(21/5)=4, floor(35/7)=5 -> 5x4x5=100
Orientation F (4 along 20, 7 along 21, 5 along 35): floor(20/4)=5, floor(21/7)=3, floor(35/5)=7 -> 5x3x7=105

questions.prompt: Q2 — After a successful pilot in Singapore, Robot Co. plans to rent out Gundam-II through monthly payments. How should they price the service, and what factors should be considered?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first brainstorm pricing factors (cost floor, value ceiling, competitive position, willingness to pay), then be given the data to compute both the cost-based and value-based numbers. Key insight: cost << value created, so a value-based pricing strategy is recommended given Robot Co.'s 2-5 year patent monopoly. The exact rental price is open but must be justified.

math.setup: Cost side: manufacturing cost SGD 9,000 per unit; useful lifespan 5 years; monthly maintenance SGD 100. Value side: average monthly server salary SGD 1,600; Gundam-II is twice as efficient per task (8 min vs 16 min); restaurants open 12 hours/day, servers work 8-hour shifts so 1.5 shifts needed; Gundam-II replaces 80% of server functions.
steps: Cost-based floor: SGD 9,000 / (12 months x 5 years) + SGD 100 = SGD 150 + SGD 100 = SGD 250 / month
Value created per server replaced: SGD 1,600 x (16 min / 8 min efficiency factor) x 1.5 shift factor x 80% replaceable = SGD 1,600 x 2 x 1.5 x 0.8 = SGD 3,840 / month
Because cost floor (SGD 250) is far below value created (SGD 3,840), value-based pricing is preferred
Proposed rental should be between SGD 250 and SGD 3,840; candidate should suggest a specific number with rationale (e.g., SGD 1,000 to share value and drive adoption)
math.answer: Cost floor: SGD 250/month; Value ceiling: SGD 3,840/month; Recommended strategy: value-based pricing, e.g., SGD 1,000/month

questions.prompt: Q3 — If Robot Co. decides to charge a monthly rental of SGD 1,000 per robot, estimate the market size of Gundam-II in Singapore. Before calculating, state the numbers you need and your key assumptions.
questions.guidance: Candidate should first identify the data needed (number of full-service restaurants, servers per restaurant, opening hours), then state assumptions (uniform restaurant size, conversion rate). The model should chain: restaurants x servers x replaceable share / shift factor / efficiency factor x conversion rate x rental x 12 months. An excellent candidate explicitly calls out the efficiency factor (Gundam-II replaces 2 human-equivalent servers per slot) and justifies the 70% adoption rate.

math.setup: Inputs: 4,000 full-service restaurants in Singapore; 15 servers per restaurant; 80% of functions replaceable; 1.5 shift factor; efficiency factor of 2 (Gundam-II = 2x faster); 70% of restaurants willing to convert; SGD 1,000 monthly rental.
steps: Robots needed per restaurant: 15 servers x 80% replaceable / 1.5 shift factor / 2 efficiency factor = 15 x 0.8 / 1.5 / 2 = 4 robots
Total robots across converting restaurants: 4,000 x 70% x 4 = 11,200 robots
Annual market size: 11,200 x SGD 1,000 x 12 = SGD 134,400,000

questions.prompt: Q4 — If Robot Co. decided to enter Singapore, what risks should it consider and how can they be mitigated?
questions.guidance: This is an open creative question. Candidates should organise risks into coherent buckets with mitigation ideas. Three major categories expected: (1) Regulation risks, (2) Gundam-II operational risks, (3) Public perception risks.

brainstorming.prompt: Q4 — What are the key risks for Robot Co. entering the Singapore market with Gundam-II, and how can they be mitigated?

categories.name: Regulation risks
ideas: Singapore food safety regulations may require certification for robots handling food
Labor laws or employment protection rules may slow adoption or attract regulatory backlash
Data privacy regulations around cameras or sensors on the robot in public spaces
Health authority approval required for self-disinfection claims

categories.name: Gundam-II operational risks
ideas: Technical failures (breakdown, software bugs) disrupting restaurant operations mid-service
Collision with customers or staff causing injury liability
Difficulty navigating varied restaurant floor plans or crowded environments
Maintenance and repair turnaround time if a unit breaks down
Battery life and charging downtime during peak hours

categories.name: Public perception risks
ideas: Customers — particularly in high-end restaurants — may prefer human interaction and resist robot service
Media or public backlash around job displacement for servers
Negative viral incidents (e.g., spills, collisions) damaging brand
Luxury restaurants may explicitly reject robot service as incompatible with their brand proposition

recommendation: Robot Co. should proceed with the Singapore market entry given no competitors for 2-5 years, growing demand for contactless dining post-Covid-19, and strong unit economics (value created SGD 3,840/month vs. cost of SGD 250/month)
Recommended pricing: value-based monthly rental of ~SGD 1,000 per robot, sharing value with restaurant clients to drive rapid adoption while capturing significant margin
Target full-service casual-dining and fast-casual restaurants first; defer luxury segment given resistance to non-human service
risks: Regulatory approval processes may delay launch timeline
Public or labour-union pushback against job displacement
Operational failures in live service environments could damage brand credibility early
next_steps: Complete regulatory due diligence with Singapore MOM and NEA on food-service robot deployment
Run a structured pilot in 3-5 restaurants across different segments to validate unit economics and customer reception
Develop a rapid-response maintenance SLA to address breakdown risk before scaling
